lessons.title: AI, GitHub and Public Publishing as Optional Tools
lessons.overview: Use AI assistance, private version control, social serialization and public repositories as separate optional choices while protecting context, consent, continuity, provenance and writer approval.
objectives: Distinguish AI-assisted, AI-generated and no-AI workflows without claiming one universal legal classification.
Use provider-independent AI with bounded context, provenance and explicit approval.
Separate private collaboration from public publishing and promotional serialization.

sections.heading: Choose the tool after defining the task
paragraphs: AI can ask questions, critique, identify evidence, compare alternatives or propose a revision for review. GitHub can preserve proposed versions and discussion. Social platforms can publish or serialize selected material. None of these tools is required to use the 24 Blocks method or write a screenplay in PlotPickle.

Avoid treating AI-assisted, AI-generated and no-AI as universal legal categories. Record what actually happened: the provider, task, supplied context, output retained, human changes and approval decision.

sections.heading: Bound context and preserve approval
paragraphs: Share the smallest canonical scope needed for the task. Do not send confidential collaborator material, private research, personal data, culturally sensitive material or third-party content without permission and a reasoned provider choice.
Keep generated output separate from the original. The writer reviews evidence, invented facts, continuity risk, voice drift and rights concerns before retaining anything.

sections.heading: Collaboration is not publication
paragraphs: A private repository supports invited collaboration. A public repository makes material visible. A social post serializes or promotes selected material. An open licence grants stated reuse permissions. These controls should never be collapsed into one public/private switch.

sections.heading: Route craft work to guided revision
paragraphs: Detailed AI craft instruction belongs in PlotPickle's AI-Assisted Revision collection from issue #49. Choose a focused pass, operation and canonical scope, then route only approved work to the relevant specialist engine or lab.

Public publishing decisions should also consider confidentiality, consent, cultural care, continuity, third-party rights, platform terms and whether early disclosure harms later submission or commercial plans.

definitions.meaning: A workflow in which a person uses an AI system for defined support while retaining responsibility for selection, revision and approval.
Only the smallest approved project material needed for the task is supplied to a provider.
Publishing a work in selected instalments or posts rather than sharing the complete private project.

example.title: Private diagnosis, no automatic rewrite
example.text: The writer sends one scene and its character goals to a chosen provider, requests critique only, records the provider and date, rejects an invented backstory and retains two questions. The screenplay remains private; nothing is posted publicly or merged automatically.

checklist: The task can be explained without naming a model brand.
The smallest canonical scope is selected.
Confidentiality, consent and provider terms are considered.
The original remains visible beside any proposal.
Retained material has provenance and explicit approval.
Private collaboration, public publishing and open licensing are separate decisions.
mistakes: Sending the complete project when one scene is enough.
Treating confident output as verified evidence.
Using a public repository for private review by accident.
Assuming a social post grants or protects rights.
Repeating generic prompt advice instead of using the guided revision playbooks.
lessons.exercise: Choose one optional tool for the active project: AI, private GitHub, public repository or social serialization. State the exact purpose, context boundary, access level, approval step and reason the other tools are not required for this task.

lessons.title: Choose the Collaboration Model
lessons.overview: Define ownership, access, proposal rights, approval authority, privacy, credit and licensing before inviting anyone.
objectives: Compare eight models.
Separate access, ownership and reuse.
Set response and confidentiality expectations.

sections.heading: The operating agreement
paragraphs: The model defines who owns the current project, who may view, comment or propose, who decides canon and what credit, compensation, ownership, confidentiality or licence expectations apply.
Ordinary collaboration may remain local-only or use file exchange. GitHub, AI, public publishing and an open licence remain optional tools and separate decisions.
points: Solo project with occasional feedback: One project owner; Local or private by default; No open licence implied.
Private reviewer access: One project owner; Confidential/private; No reuse right implied.
Invited contributor: One project owner; Defined by the brief; Only recorded permission applies.
Co-writing partnership: Shared or agreement-defined; Usually private during development; Joint licensing requires relevant owners.
Commissioned rewrite or specialist service: Commissioning party or agreement-defined; Usually confidential; Contract or permission controls reuse.
Production-team collaboration: Producer, company or agreement-defined; Production policy; Asset-specific permission required.
Public feedback project: Named project owner; Public material only; Separate explicit licence decision.
Openly licensed community project: Named owner or governance group; Public; Recorded open licence governs covered material only.

definitions.meaning: The agreed structure for access, contribution, authority, privacy, credit, ownership and reuse.

example.title: Private reader versus open community
example.text: Both may use PlotPickle; only the second uses explicit open contributor terms.

mistakes: Assuming feedback creates ownership.
Confusing public visibility with reuse permission.
lessons.exercise: Choose the active project's collaboration model.

lessons.title: Define Roles and Decision Authority
lessons.overview: Translate creative roles into an authority matrix without confusing them with GitHub permissions.
objectives: Define roles.
Assign authority.
Separate technical permission.

sections.heading: Responsibility and enforcement
paragraphs: A role states what someone is asked to do and may decide. Technical permission states what an account can do.
The owner retains final canon authority unless a written agreement establishes shared or delegated authority.
points: Project Owner: Controls canon, repository connection, rights settings and final acceptance unless a written agreement shares authority.
Co-owner / Maintainer: May share final approval, licence or invitation authority only when explicitly authorized.
Writer / Co-writer: Creates story or screenplay material within an agreed scope; ownership and approval remain separate questions.
Contributor: Proposes bounded additions or changes without automatically controlling canon.
Reviewer: Comments and identifies questions without changing the approved project.
Story Editor: Diagnoses and recommends revisions but does not automatically own, approve or merge them.
Research / Continuity Contributor: Supplies sourced facts, canon checks or continuity findings with provenance.
Visual, Music or Production Contributor: Supplies specialist assets with permission, credit and provenance information.

sections.heading: Authority matrix
paragraphs: Record view, comment, thread, proposal, rights, asset, merge, licence and invitation authority.
points: Authority choice: Invite or remove collaborators

definitions.meaning: The agreed right to make a project decision.
The capability to perform an action in a tool.

example.title: Story editor with write access
example.text: The editor may propose while the owner still decides canon.

mistakes: Assuming write access means merge authority.
lessons.exercise: Audit one collaborator's authority.

lessons.title: Create a Contribution Brief
lessons.overview: Turn an open invitation into a bounded assignment with purpose, locks, freedom, rights and acceptance criteria.
objectives: Name the problem.
Anchor the target.
Record continuity and rights.

sections.heading: Brief the work
paragraphs: Name the contributor, role, decision-maker, target, problem, audience effect, canon locks, elements that must not change, output, freedom, due date, review window, sharing, credit, compensation, ownership, licence and acceptance criteria.
points: Template: Storyboard, music or production asset

definitions.meaning: A structured request defining scope, purpose, locks, deliverable, rights and acceptance.

example.title: Alternative crisis scene
example.text: The brief locks earlier facts and requires a changed choice with a new consequence.

mistakes: Asking someone to improve the story.
Discussing ownership only after acceptance.
lessons.exercise: Create one brief for the active selection.

lessons.title: Start From the Approved Story
lessons.overview: Pull or exchange the approved project, work locally and submit a bounded proposal instead of writing directly to canon.
objectives: Identify the approved base.
Work locally.
Handle stale bases deliberately.

sections.heading: Safe sequence
paragraphs: Pull the approved canonical version for review, compare and deliberately apply it, read the brief and locks, work locally, save backups and submit a bounded proposal. Local-only and file-based collaboration remain fully supported.
A stale base requires a newly approved pull and human reconsideration; complete creative versions cannot always be mechanically merged.
points: Approved story → local draft → proposal → review → decision → canon.

definitions.meaning: A proposal based on an older canonical revision.

example.title: Another ending merged first
example.text: Pull the new canon and reconsider causality, character and continuity before resubmitting.

mistakes: Writing directly to canon.
Forcing a creative merge.
lessons.exercise: Identify the next proposal's exact scope.

lessons.title: Submit a Reviewable Proposal
lessons.overview: Package purpose, scope, evidence, dependencies, questions and provenance before opening GitHub.
objectives: Explain what changed.
Name dependencies.
Surface rights and questions.

sections.heading: Proposal packet
paragraphs: Explain what changed and why, audience effect, exact areas, source brief, before-and-after evidence, consequences for characters, continuity, Story Threads, runtime, production and rights, new assumptions, unresolved questions, alternatives, provenance, credit and inspection areas.
The proposal must be understandable inside PlotPickle before the owner opens GitHub.

definitions.meaning: Creative context for a reviewable change.

example.title: Dialogue pass
example.text: The packet identifies changed scenes, relationship effects, a new canon fact and a permission question.

mistakes: Using only a vague proposal title.
Hiding canon assumptions.
lessons.exercise: Create a packet for the active local change.

lessons.title: Review the Change, Not the Person
lessons.overview: Anchor evidence-based feedback, categorize its purpose and separate project requirements from preference.
objectives: Categorize feedback.
Anchor comments.
Close the loop.

sections.heading: Evidence first
paragraphs: Anchor to a story field, Block, scene, screenplay element or character. Describe audience experience or factual conflict before prescribing a fix. Explain reason and intended outcome and acknowledge retained strengths.
Act and Block questions are optional lenses that adapt to the active structure; they do not impose one fixed legacy Act model.

definitions.meaning: A review note linked to a canonical project element.

example.title: Continuity before prescription
example.text: Mark when a character cannot know a fact and name the intended audience uncertainty.

mistakes: Reviewing the person.
Treating taste as a requirement.
lessons.exercise: Create one anchored review note.

lessons.title: Decide, Disagree and Record Canon
lessons.overview: Separate discussion, approval and canon and record merge, decline, defer, withdraw or supersede decisions.
objectives: Use a decision lifecycle.
Resolve disagreements by evidence.
Record rationale.

sections.heading: Explicit decision
paragraphs: Local draft → proposal → review → changes requested or approved → owner/maintainer merge → canonical pull.

Restate the goal and brief, isolate the disagreement, separate continuity from preference, compare audience effect, causality, character, theme, feasibility and rights, identify final authority and record the decision.

definitions.meaning: A dated outcome, decision-maker, rationale, rights update and follow-up record.

example.title: Two climax approaches
example.text: Test both, choose under the authority model and preserve the declined proposal history.

mistakes: Assuming consensus is required.
Closing without a reason.
lessons.exercise: Record one proposal decision.

lessons.title: Record Credit, Ownership and Permissions
lessons.overview: Connect accepted work to contributor, agreement, ownership, licence, permission and provenance records.
objectives: Record the contributor.
Separate contribution and ownership.
Link accepted work.

sections.heading: Rights distinctions
paragraphs: Feedback does not automatically create ownership. A contribution does not automatically transfer copyright. A pull request is not an employment, assignment or licence agreement. A public repository is not an open licence. PlotPickle software and documentation licences do not automatically apply to the user's screenplay.
Record name, credited-as name, role, contribution, ownership share if any, compensation or commissioned status when documented, agreement or permission reference, linked work and acceptance date.

definitions.meaning: A pointer to written terms governing role, payment, ownership, credit or permission.

example.title: Accepted storyboard frames
example.text: Record artist, asset IDs, fee agreement, permission and acceptance date.

mistakes: Treating a pull request as copyright transfer.
lessons.exercise: Audit one accepted contribution.

lessons.title: Protect Privacy and Scale the Review Queue
lessons.overview: Keep unfinished work private and scale through briefs, area owners, statuses, dependencies and explicit canon decisions.
objectives: Protect local work.
Set review capacity.
Scale bounded proposals.

sections.heading: Privacy and scale
paragraphs: Local drafts, autosaves, AI prompts and private assets do not leave the computer merely because GitHub is connected. Credentials remain outside the .ppf. Only intentionally submitted proposal material is shared.

Assign briefs, define review owners, limit simultaneous high-risk proposals, track dependencies, group review rounds, archive superseded work and publish realistic response expectations. Unlimited Contributions remains searchable, but projects may define capacity, deadlines and closed areas.
points: Community feedback is not automatically an authorized contribution.
GitHub manages the technical queue; PlotPickle presents creative-project meaning.

definitions.meaning: The realistic volume and timing a project can assess.

example.title: Production team
example.text: Area leads review visual, audio, continuity and screenplay briefs while the canon path stays short.

mistakes: Promising detailed feedback on every submission.
Uploading third-party material without authority.
lessons.exercise: Define privacy, review owners and proposal limits.

lessons.title: Build the Character Engine
lessons.overview: Connect want, need, Ghost, protective lie, emerging truth, strengths, liabilities, strategy, stakes and contradiction into one playable dramatic engine.
objectives: Separate a conscious want from an underlying need.
Translate backstory into present behaviour and access.
Define a strategy that can be pressured and changed on screen.

sections.heading: Start with the active strategy
paragraphs: A character is not a biography. The useful question is what the person does now to pursue safety, belonging, control, love, status, justice or another need. The current strategy should explain repeated choices while leaving room for contradiction.
points: Want: the result the character consciously pursues.
Need: the truth or capacity required for deeper change.
Ghost: a formative condition still shaping present interpretation.
Protective lie: the belief that makes the current strategy feel necessary.
Emerging truth: the understanding that pressure may prove or reject.

sections.heading: Make strengths double-edged
paragraphs: A strength becomes dramatic when the same capacity that helps in one condition creates cost in another. Loyalty may become complicity; decisiveness may become control; empathy may become avoidance of necessary conflict.
points: Name the condition where it works.
Name the condition where it becomes a liability.
Show the cost through a choice rather than a label.

sections.heading: Use backstory only when it acts
paragraphs: Keep backstory that changes what the character notices, fears, knows, can access, withholds, risks or chooses. A fact that never affects present action may be interesting to the writer but is not yet part of the screenplay engine.

definitions.meaning: A limiting belief that makes the character's current survival strategy feel reasonable.
The more accurate understanding the story may test, prove, complicate or reject.
Expressed through observable behaviour, choice, dialogue, silence, access or consequence.

example.title: A strength under the wrong pressure
example.text: Mara's reliability wins trust at work, but she treats every relationship like a duty roster. When her brother asks for honest disagreement rather than rescue, reliability becomes control until she risks letting him choose badly.

checklist: The protective lie explains the current strategy.
The character contains a useful contradiction.
The engine can be tested by visible choices.
mistakes: Writing biography without present consequence.
Treating flaw as a moral insult.
Making need a second external goal.
Explaining the arc before dramatizing it.
lessons.exercise: Choose one active character. Complete the sentence: Because of the Ghost, they believe ____, so when pressured they usually ____. Name one strength that helps this strategy and one condition where it becomes costly.

lessons.title: Prove Character Through Choice
lessons.overview: Turn profile claims into a chain of condition, objective, options, pressure, tactic, choice, consequence and changed strategy.
objectives: Find character evidence in Blocks, scenes, mini-blocks and screenplay elements.
Distinguish a stated trait from a pressured choice.
Design increasingly costly proof without requiring a positive transformation.

sections.heading: Build the evidence chain
paragraphs: Character becomes visible when the audience can compare what was available with what the person chose. A useful evidence chain records the condition, objective, meaningful options, pressure, tactic, decision, consequence and next strategy.
points: Condition: what is true at the start of the movement.
Objective: what the character tries to change now.
Options: at least two live courses of action.
Choice: the selected action or refusal.
Consequence: the new pressure created by that decision.

sections.heading: Raise the cost, not only the volume
paragraphs: An arc does not require louder versions of the same obstacle. Strong proof removes excuses, increases personal cost, changes who is watching or forces the character to sacrifice one value to protect another.

sections.heading: Compare plan with draft
paragraphs: Use the Character Proof dashboard to compare profile and Arc Matrix claims with linked Blocks, scenes, mini-blocks, checkpoints and screenplay character cues. Gaps are questions for the writer, not permission for automatic rewriting.

definitions.meaning: A linked story event that demonstrates a belief, strategy, choice, consequence, relationship shift or voice pattern.
A decision that risks or sacrifices something the character values.
A new method of pursuit produced by prior pressure and consequence.

example.title: The same belief at three costs
example.text: At first, Eli hides a mistake to protect his job. Later he lets a colleague take blame to protect promotion. At crisis, he must either repeat the strategy and endanger a patient or confess publicly. The cost progression proves the belief before the final choice tests change.

checklist: More than one option is live.
Later evidence increases cost or removes an excuse.
The ending proof can be compared with the opening strategy.
mistakes: Calling a feeling an action.
Using a final speech as the only proof of change.
Treating all evidence as equally important.
Letting diagnostics rewrite scenes automatically.
lessons.exercise: Find one current Block or scene containing the selected character. Write the objective, live options, choice and consequence. Then identify what belief or strategy the evidence supports or contradicts.

lessons.title: Map the Inner Journey Without Forcing It
lessons.overview: Use flexible opening, catalyst, threshold, midpoint, crisis, climax, ending and custom checkpoints across positive, flat, negative, tragic, ambiguous and ensemble arcs.
objectives: Choose an intended arc shape without treating it as a mandatory template.
Use checkpoints as evidence locations rather than fixed page prescriptions.
Ask act-specific questions that adapt to the active character and story position.

sections.heading: Choose the shape, then test it
paragraphs: An arc shape communicates intention; it does not guarantee what the draft proves. Positive transformation is only one option. A steadfast character may hold a truth, a tragic character may refuse it, and an ensemble may distribute change across relationships.
points: Positive transformation: The character replaces a limiting strategy with a more truthful and effective one.
Steadfast or flat: The character holds a tested truth and changes the people or system around them.
Negative or corruption: Pressure rewards a damaging strategy until the character embraces it.
Disillusionment: The character loses a false belief, but the truth may be painful rather than liberating.
Tragic refusal: The character reaches the decisive truth or choice and refuses it at a cost.
Recovery or reconciliation: Change is demonstrated through repair, renewed trust or a sustainable new practice.
Incomplete or ambiguous: The ending provides mixed evidence, partial change or an intentionally unresolved condition.
Ensemble or relationship: Change is distributed across a group or becomes visible through how a relationship reorganizes.
Describe your own: Use the checkpoints without forcing the story into a named arc pattern.

sections.heading: Use flexible checkpoints
paragraphs: Opening, catalyst, threshold, midpoint, crisis, climax and ending are useful comparison points because they reveal strategy under changing pressure. Custom checkpoints are equally valid when the story's form requires them.

sections.heading: Let the active story choose the questions
paragraphs: Characters in Motion recommends questions from the selected act, Block, scene and checkpoint. The questions diagnose evidence; they do not require a Hero's Journey or fixed Block assignment.

definitions.meaning: The intended pattern of change, refusal, steadfastness, recovery, ambiguity or distributed relationship movement.
A chosen story position used to record belief, strategy, pressure, choice, consequence and evidence.
The decisive action that demonstrates change, steadfastness, corruption, refusal or unresolved contradiction.

example.title: A flat arc with relationship change
example.text: Nadia begins and ends believing the institution must tell the truth. Her checkpoints do not show belief reversal; they show increasing cost, smarter tactics and the gradual conversion of two colleagues who initially oppose her.

checklist: The arc shape is optional and editable.
Checkpoints follow the story rather than a rigid page map.
Crisis and climax choices are distinct.
The ending state includes relationship or world impact.
Ambiguity is deliberate rather than missing information.
mistakes: Forcing every character into positive transformation.
Treating midpoint as a page number only.
Writing checkpoint summaries without linked evidence.
Confusing an incomplete arc with an unfinished draft.
lessons.exercise: Select an intended arc shape. Choose the checkpoint nearest the active Block and record belief, strategy, pressure, choice, consequence and one linked piece of evidence.

lessons.title: Join Inner and Outer Conflict
lessons.overview: Connect external obstacles to the belief, fear, desire, moral cost and relationship strategy they expose in this specific character.
objectives: Modernize conflict categories into playable pressures.
Make the same obstacle produce different choices for different characters.
Link internal conflict to action, refusal, language, risk and consequence.

sections.heading: Use a pressure spectrum
paragraphs: Conflict may arise from self, another person, a relationship, a group, an institution, a system, environment, technology, time, history, fate or social expectation. The category matters less than how the character interprets and answers it.
points: Self versus belief, fear, desire or moral cost.
Person versus group, institution or system.
Person versus technology or constructed system.
Person versus time, history, fate or social expectation.

sections.heading: Make internal conflict playable
paragraphs: Thoughts and feelings become screenplay conflict when they change what the character notices, withholds, says, refuses, risks or does. An internal dilemma needs live options with meaningful costs.

sections.heading: Connect pressure to consequence
paragraphs: External pressure should expose or reward the current strategy. Consequence then changes the next available choice, preventing conflict from becoming a sequence of unrelated obstacles.

definitions.meaning: Competing beliefs, desires, loyalties or moral costs that alter observable behaviour.
Resistance in the world that blocks, redirects or raises the cost of an objective.
An obstacle whose meaning and available response depend on this person's history, values, skills and relationships.

example.title: One deadline, two characters
example.text: A storm traps a rescue team. For the leader, the deadline pressures control and responsibility; for the medic, it pressures a promise never to abandon one patient. The same weather produces incompatible choices because it activates different strategies.

checklist: The internal dilemma has live options.
Conflict is not reduced to argument alone.
mistakes: Leaving internal conflict entirely in thought.
Using generic obstacles unrelated to character.
Repeating the same argument without changed stakes.
Treating a category name as a scene.
lessons.exercise: Take the active Block's conflict. Explain what it means specifically to the selected character, which strategy it activates, the live alternative and the consequence of each option.

lessons.title: Build Opposition as a Competing Worldview
lessons.overview: Design protagonists, antagonists, rivals, foils and systems around incompatible objectives and persuasive working beliefs rather than simple villain labels.
objectives: Give the opposing force agency and self-justification.
Use thesis, antithesis and synthesis as an optional lens.
Distinguish moral equivalence from dramatic credibility.

sections.heading: Start with incompatible objectives
paragraphs: Opposition becomes active when another person, group, system or condition pursues an objective that cannot coexist with the protagonist's current course. The opposing force should be able to initiate action rather than merely react.
points: Evidence that makes each position persuasive to its holder.
Changed understanding, unresolved tension or tragic refusal.

sections.heading: Use the dialectical lens carefully
paragraphs: Starting belief → counter-pressure → changed understanding is the plain-language version of thesis, antithesis and synthesis. The story may end with synthesis, rejection, stalemate or tragedy; it does not need to declare both sides equally moral.

sections.heading: Let foils reveal strategy
paragraphs: A foil is useful when a contrasting strategy makes the protagonist's choices legible. It is a temporary dramatic function, not a complete identity or required cast slot.

definitions.meaning: A person, group, system or condition with agency or pressure that blocks the current objective.
A character whose contrasting strategy makes another character's choices easier to perceive.
An optional lens comparing a starting position, counter-position and resulting changed understanding.

example.title: Credible does not mean equivalent
example.text: The inspector believes secrecy prevents panic; the journalist believes secrecy enables abuse. Both have evidence and agency, but the screenplay can still judge the inspector's coercion as harmful while understanding why he chooses it.

checklist: The opposing force has an objective.
The protagonist is pressured to adapt.
Foils reveal strategy rather than replace specificity.
The ending resolves or deliberately preserves the argument.
mistakes: Writing an antagonist who only waits for the hero.
Confusing credibility with moral equivalence.
Treating archetype as personality.
Forcing a neat synthesis onto a tragic or unresolved ending.
lessons.exercise: Write the protagonist's working belief and the strongest counter-position in the active story. Give each one concrete evidence, an objective and one action that escalates incompatibility.

lessons.title: Design Relationships That Change Both People
lessons.overview: Define each relationship from both directions, track power and withheld needs, and connect change to shared scenes and arc checkpoints.
objectives: Compare what each person wants from the other.
Track status, history, recurring tactics and turning events.
Use relationship change as character evidence rather than decoration.

sections.heading: Write both perspectives
paragraphs: A relationship is not one shared paragraph. Each person assigns the other a role, wants something different and interprets the same history through a different need. PlotPickle can compare the selected character's relationship record with the reciprocal record on the other character.
points: What each wants from the other.
The role each assigns the other.

sections.heading: Track the turning event
paragraphs: A relationship changes when an action alters trust, debt, status, access, expectation or dependence. Link the turning event to a scene, Block or checkpoint so the change can be verified in the story.

sections.heading: Allow adaptation in both directions
paragraphs: One person's change should force the other to adapt, resist, exploit, grieve or reconsider. The resulting relationship may strengthen, rupture, reverse, stabilize or remain unresolved.

definitions.meaning: The second character's separate description of the same relationship.
A repeated method used to gain closeness, control, approval, distance, truth or another relational objective.
An action that changes trust, status, access, debt, expectation or dependence.

example.title: Two descriptions, one marriage
example.text: Lena describes Sam as the person she must protect from risk. Sam describes Lena as the person who uses protection to avoid being known. Their midpoint scene changes both perspectives when Sam accepts a danger Lena cannot control.

checklist: A turning event is linked to story evidence.
The ending condition reflects both characters' adaptation.
mistakes: Using one shared relationship description.
Treating conflict as proof of depth.
Writing chemistry without objectives or tactics.
Changing one character while the other remains mechanically unchanged.
lessons.exercise: Choose a relationship. Write one sentence from each person's perspective, identify the current power balance and name the next event that could change trust, status or dependence.

lessons.title: Give Every Character a Playable Voice
lessons.overview: Build voice from worldview, attention, rhythm, vocabulary, verbal fingerprints, emotional access, status shifts, persuasion, silence and relationship pressure.
objectives: Distinguish voice from accent or demographic shorthand.
Test Voiceprint claims against screenplay dialogue evidence.
Research language communities with specificity and informed human review.

sections.heading: Voice begins before dialogue
paragraphs: Voice includes what the character notices, how they frame causality, which emotions they permit, how they manage status and what they do instead of speaking. Dialogue is one expression of a larger strategy.

sections.heading: Change voice by relationship and pressure
paragraphs: A playable Voiceprint is stable enough to recognize and flexible enough to respond to status, intimacy, danger and concealment. Compare how the same character speaks to an authority, rival, dependent and trusted friend.

sections.heading: Research without certification claims
paragraphs: Avoid phonetic spelling and demographic shortcuts as substitutes for a person. Research variation within language communities, power, context and consent. AI can suggest questions or flag patterns, but it cannot certify lived experience or replace informed human review.

definitions.meaning: A set of repeatable language, attention, rhythm, emotional and persuasion patterns that remain responsive to context.
A recurring phrase shape, avoidance pattern, metaphor family or conversational move associated with the character.
Dialogue shaped to feel credible while still serving screenplay pace, conflict and clarity.

example.title: Status changes sentence shape
example.text: With staff, Omar speaks in clipped decisions. With his mother, he over-explains and asks permission. Under public accusation, both patterns collide: short denials followed by a flood of justification.

checklist: Voice changes by relationship and pressure.
Representation questions receive informed human review.
mistakes: Reducing voice to accent.
Using demographic labels as dialogue instructions.
Making every line equally polished.
Asking AI to certify authenticity.
lessons.exercise: Select one character and two relationships. Write the same refusal to each person, changing status, emotional access, rhythm, vocabulary and what remains unsaid while preserving the character's core worldview.

lessons.title: Design the Cast as a Dramatic System
lessons.overview: Treat archetypes as optional functions, audit cast economy and identify redundant or underpowered roles without automatically merging characters.
objectives: Assign multiple flexible dramatic functions to characters.
Identify cast redundancy as a writer question.
Modernize dated labels into agency, vulnerability and story-function language.

sections.heading: Use functions, not identity boxes
paragraphs: Protagonist, opposing force, ally, pressure ally, foil, mentor, challenger, witness, beneficiary, victim, relationship carrier, subplot carrier, tonal counterforce and community representative are temporary dramatic functions. One character may carry several and a function may transfer or reverse.
points: Witness, beneficiary or victim of choices.

sections.heading: Audit cast economy
paragraphs: Compare the functions, Story Threads, Blocks and scenes carried by each character. Two thin characters may be redundant, or they may need stronger distinctions. The audit should ask questions and preserve writer ownership rather than automatically merging roles.
points: Who exists only to approve the protagonist?
Which characters have no consequential scene evidence?

sections.heading: Modernize vulnerability and rescue
paragraphs: Replace labels such as Damsel with neutral analysis: who has agency, who is endangered, who creates the rescue plan, who pays the cost and how vulnerability changes relationships. A vulnerable character can remain active; a powerful character can still require rescue.

sections.heading: Do not promise commercial outcomes
paragraphs: Self-sacrifice, antiheroes, forbidden love and other familiar patterns can shape audience experience, but no character device guarantees profitability, recognition or production. Execution, context and the complete work matter.
points: Representation requires specificity, agency, research and informed review.
AI may surface questions but cannot certify authenticity or commercial potential.

definitions.meaning: A temporary job a character performs in the dramatic system.
The balance between distinct character value and the complexity or repetition created by the size of the cast.
Evidence that two characters may perform the same function without meaningful contrast, consequence or relationship value.

example.title: Keep both or combine?
example.text: Two detectives deliver clues and agree with the lead. The audit asks whether one can become a procedural loyalist and the other a moral challenger. If no distinct pressure, relationship or thread emerges, combining them becomes a writer option—not an automatic instruction.

checklist: Every major character initiates or changes something.
Foils have specific lives beyond contrast.
Thin roles are questioned rather than deleted automatically.
No craft pattern is presented as a profitability guarantee.
mistakes: Treating archetypes as identities.
Filling required cast slots mechanically.
Using dated gendered labels.
Merging characters without reviewing relationships, rights or continuity.
Claiming a character device predicts commercial success.
lessons.exercise: List each active character's two most important functions, linked Story Threads and consequential scenes. Identify one missing function and one possible redundancy, then write the question you need to answer before changing the cast.

lessons.title: Dialogue Is Action
lessons.overview: Treat every exchange as behaviour: speech, silence and physical action used to pursue an objective under pressure.
objectives: Map objectives, tactics and resistance.
Track information and leverage.
End with a changed condition.

sections.heading: The playable exchange
paragraphs: A line is not merely information. It may pressure, evade, seduce, test, accuse, bargain, distract, conceal, provoke, reassure, recruit, threaten, surrender or change the subject.

Begin with relationship condition, each objective, each belief about the other, tactic, resistance, information held or withheld, status, spoken action, physical action, turn and changed exit condition.
points: Possible spoken or silent action: pressure
Possible spoken or silent action: evade
Possible spoken or silent action: reveal
Possible spoken or silent action: conceal
Possible spoken or silent action: test
Possible spoken or silent action: persuade
Possible spoken or silent action: threaten
Possible spoken or silent action: bond
Possible spoken or silent action: deflect
Possible spoken or silent action: explain
Possible spoken or silent action: joke
Possible spoken or silent action: surrender
Possible spoken or silent action: change topic
Possible spoken or silent action: silence/reaction

sections.heading: Selected reality
paragraphs: Realistic dialogue is selected reality. Literal conversation contains filler, repetition and dead space; screenplay naturalism shapes truthful behaviour for purpose, rhythm and performance.
Not every line must advance plot. A line may reveal relationship, regulate pace, establish tone, create anticipation, release pressure or make later action meaningful.

definitions.meaning: The playable strategy used to pursue an immediate objective.
What is materially different when the exchange ends.

example.title: The request that becomes a test
example.text: A character asks for a ride, but the actual objective is to test whether an estranged sibling will show up. A delayed answer changes the relationship before either discusses it directly.

checklist: The exit differs from the entry.
mistakes: Using dialogue only to transfer facts.
Polishing isolated lines before designing the exchange.
Equating realism with transcription.
lessons.exercise: Create a Dialogue Blueprint for the active scene or mini-block and label the first tactic, resistance and turn.

lessons.title: Build a Playable Voiceprint
lessons.overview: Connect Voiceprint tendencies to perception, rhythm, vocabulary, emotional access, status and persuasion without reducing voice to accent or catchphrase.
objectives: Turn character fields into playable tendencies.
Compare voices with evidence.
Allow motivated variation.

sections.heading: Voice is perception plus strategy
paragraphs: Voice is what a character notices, how they organize thought and how they try to affect another person. Use sentence rhythm, vocabulary and metaphor families, directness, humour and defence, emotional access, silence patterns, persuasion and status behaviour.
A believable voice changes with audience, power, fear, intimacy, deception, exhaustion and growth. Consistency does not mean sameness.

sections.heading: Accent and dialect require care
paragraphs: Do not use phonetic spelling or demographic shorthand as a substitute for character. Prioritize researched syntax, vocabulary, rhythm, worldview and context, and seek informed human review where appropriate.
AI may surface comparison questions but cannot certify cultural authenticity or imitate a real performer without permission.

definitions.meaning: A flexible pattern of perception, language and strategy supported by screenplay evidence.

example.title: Shared profession, different tactic
example.text: Two surgeons share technical vocabulary. One compresses language to control status; the other uses precise questions to slow decisions and expose risk.

mistakes: Treating accent as voice.
Flagging every variation as inconsistency.
Repeating catchphrases mechanically.
lessons.exercise: Compare two active characters across rhythm, directness, metaphor, emotional access, status and persuasion, then find supporting lines.

lessons.title: Write Subtext and Withheld Information
lessons.overview: Create subtext from objectives, relationships, protected facts and the cost of direct speech rather than cryptic wording.
objectives: Separate spoken and private subjects.
Track audience knowledge and interpretation.
Design reveal or misread turns.

sections.heading: The pressure system
paragraphs: Map the spoken subject, actual objective, hidden feeling or belief, protected fact, audience knowledge, the other character's interpretation, cost of direct speech, indirect tactic and reveal, misread or turn.
Use irony, avoidance, deflection, euphemism, implication, denial, testing, strategic misunderstanding and behaviour that contradicts the words. Not every line needs hidden meaning.

definitions.meaning: Meaning created by the gap among words, objective, feeling, knowledge and behaviour.

example.title: Talking about the thermostat
example.text: A couple debates room temperature while testing who still expects to share the house. Moving a suitcase becomes the actual answer.

checklist: A direct statement has a cost.
The audience can track enough meaning.
mistakes: Making every line obscure.
Adding vague pauses instead of playable evidence.
Confusing withheld information with arbitrary concealment.
lessons.exercise: Write the public topic and private subject for the active exchange, then identify one protected fact and one visible contradiction.

lessons.title: Create Conflict Without Constant Arguments
lessons.overview: Build dialogue conflict from incompatible objectives, unequal knowledge, status, affection, delay, refusal and changing tactics.
objectives: Broaden conflict beyond shouting.
Escalate by changing conditions.
Use relationship cost.

sections.heading: Conflict can be polite
paragraphs: Agreement may conceal conflict; politeness may be a weapon; silence may be refusal; affection may increase the cost of disagreement. Use incompatible objectives, competing interpretations, unequal information, moral disagreement, negotiation, lies, half-truths, refusal, delay and changing tactics.
Escalation should alter leverage, cost, exposure, time, relationship or available options, not only volume.

definitions.meaning: Information, status, access, need or consequence that changes available choices.

example.title: The friendly interview
example.text: A detective remains courteous while narrowing the witness's options. The escalation is a revealed photograph, not louder speech.

mistakes: Making every conflict an argument.
Repeating the same tactic louder.
Using hostility where strategic agreement is stronger.
lessons.exercise: Identify the active exchange's incompatible objectives and design one escalation that changes options rather than volume.

lessons.title: Balance Speech, Silence and Physical Action
lessons.overview: Use visible behaviour, reactions, tasks, interruption, distance and silence as parts of the exchange and teach accurate screenplay form.
objectives: Replace unnecessary speech with action.
Make silence playable.
Use screenplay elements correctly.

sections.heading: The answer may be physical
paragraphs: Action can change a line's meaning or replace it. Silence may be refusal, processing, control, fear, intimacy, judgement or uncertainty. Props, tasks, entrances, exits, distance, interruptions, overlap and unfinished thoughts can carry pressure.
Avoid abstract instructions such as an awkward silence when a withheld action, changed distance or delayed answer can make the event playable.

sections.heading: Screenplay form
paragraphs: Character cues identify the speaker. Dialogue contains spoken text. Action lines carry visible behaviour. Parentheticals are brief and necessary. Extensions clarify off-screen or voice-over delivery when needed. Dual dialogue indicates simultaneous speech. Prose tags such as he said or she asked are generally not screenplay dialogue formatting.
Write a pause only when the dramatic event matters, not as routine performance control.

definitions.meaning: The screenplay element identifying who speaks.
A brief, necessary performance or delivery clarification.
Two speeches formatted to occur simultaneously.

example.title: The unsigned form
example.text: Instead of saying I don't trust you, the character caps the pen and slides the form back.

mistakes: Writing he said in screenplay dialogue.
Using parentheticals for every emotion.
Calling silence awkward without evidence.
lessons.exercise: Replace one explanatory line with a visible reaction or task, then verify character cue, action, parenthetical and dialogue formatting.

lessons.title: Handle Exposition, World and Genre
lessons.overview: Attach needed information to conflict, task, urgency and relationship while using genre as pressure rather than a voice stereotype.
objectives: Determine what is needed now.
Reveal rules through use and consequence.
Avoid genre stereotypes.

sections.heading: Information under pressure
paragraphs: Identify what the audience must know now, who wants it understood, hidden, distorted or acted upon, and whether both characters already know it. Attach information to conflict, task, urgency, misunderstanding or consequence.
Reveal world rules through use and consequence. Repeat crucial information through changed meaning rather than identical explanation.

sections.heading: Genre affects pressure
paragraphs: Comedy may use rhythm, reversal, status and consequence; horror denial, incomplete knowledge, dread and silence; thriller concealment, interrogation, clocks and unstable alliances; romance desire, vulnerability, avoidance and changing intimacy; speculative stories unfamiliar terms with clear human objectives.
Genre does not dictate one dialogue style. Comedy is not always banter, drama need not be formal and science fiction does not require jargon.

definitions.meaning: Information the audience needs to understand story conditions, choices or consequences.
A concentration of information detached from active dramatic need.

example.title: A rule revealed by failure
example.text: Instead of explaining the city's memory tax, a character attempts a purchase and loses access to a sibling's name.

mistakes: Characters explaining shared facts.
Using jargon instead of objective.
Making every comedy line witty.
lessons.exercise: Find one explanatory exchange and attach its essential information to an objective, task or consequence.

lessons.title: Shape the Exchange and Scene Turn
lessons.overview: Design complete dialogue movements—entry tension, tactic, resistance, tactic change, reveal, status shift, irreversible action, turn and exit consequence.
objectives: Plan the movement.
Handle group patterns.
Link to scene and Story Thread turns.

sections.heading: Movement before polish
paragraphs: Plan the entry question or tension, first tactic, response and resistance, tactic change, reveal or misinterpretation, status shift, irreversible line or action, turn and exit question or consequence.
Two-person, ensemble, interrogation, argument, confession, negotiation, seduction, comic, remote, overlapping and one-sided conversations are patterns, not formulas.

definitions.meaning: The point where leverage, understanding, commitment or relationship condition changes.

example.title: Group agreement that isolates one person
example.text: A planning meeting appears cooperative until each practical concession removes the protagonist's authority.

mistakes: Polishing lines without a turn.
Giving every participant the same understanding.
Ending when the facts are delivered.
lessons.exercise: Map the active scene from entry tension to exit consequence and mark the irreversible line or action.

lessons.title: Revise for Voice, Purpose and Performance
lessons.overview: Diagnose the exchange before rewriting, then use focused passes for purpose, tactic, voice, subtext, exposition, status, action, rhythm, continuity and performance.
objectives: Run bounded passes.
Use evidence-based diagnostics.
Preserve original and approval controls.

sections.heading: Twelve focused passes
paragraphs: Review purpose and movement; objective and tactic; voice separation; subtext; exposition and repetition; status and escalation; action and silence; rhythm and breath; concision; continuity, arc and relationship; formatting and production clarity; read-aloud response.
A diagnostic question is not a universal failure rule. A long speech, repeated phrase, dialogue-heavy scene or shared vocabulary may be deliberate and effective.

sections.heading: Manual and optional AI workflows
paragraphs: Writers can perform every pass manually. AI suggestions must be optional, bounded and reviewable. Preserve the original, proposed version, explanation, affected continuity, provenance and explicit approve/discard controls.
Synthetic voices must remain optional and must not imitate a real performer without permission.
points: Critique only: Diagnose purpose, objective, voice, subtext, status, action and scene movement. Do not rewrite.
Voice separation: Compare rhythm, vocabulary, directness, metaphor, humour, emotional access and persuasion. Preserve deliberate shared language.
Objective and tactic: Clarify what each participant wants, the tactic used, resistance and the tactic change.
Subtext: Strengthen the gap between public topic, actual objective, protected fact and cost of direct speech without making every line cryptic.
Status and leverage: Track status at entry, leverage changes, exposure, options and the resulting turn.
Conflict escalation: Escalate through changed conditions, cost, information, relationship or available options rather than volume alone.
Exposition reduction: Keep only information needed now and attach it to conflict, task, urgency, misunderstanding or consequence.
Action and silence alternatives: Find visible behaviour, reaction, interruption, task, distance, entrance or exit that can carry meaning without explanatory speech.
Rhythm and concision: Improve exchange rhythm, interruption, breath, readability and performance while preserving purposeful release or repetition.
Genre expectation: Support the intended audience experience through pressure and information control without imposing a genre stereotype.
Continuity and arc consistency: Check facts, relationship state, Voiceprint tendencies and arc evidence while allowing motivated variation under pressure.
Compare two approaches: Offer two materially different playable strategies, explain tradeoffs and keep the original separate.

definitions.meaning: A focused diagnostic or revision operation with a defined craft goal.
A performance-oriented reading used to test clarity, rhythm, intention and response.

example.title: Diagnose before cutting
example.text: A repeated line appears redundant until the table read shows that its third use reverses status and completes a motif.

mistakes: Cutting every line that does not advance plot.
Applying AI output automatically.
Treating diagnostic counts as grades.
lessons.exercise: Run one guided pass on the selected exchange, read it aloud and record what changed in objective, tactic, rhythm or performance.

lessons.title: Build the Story Experience
lessons.overview: Connect premise, genre, audience, tone, emotional promise and the ending after-effect before choosing techniques.
objectives: Define the audience contract.
Separate plot, story, structure, style and theme.
Create a compact Story Experience Card.

sections.heading: Whose experience is this?
paragraphs: Define whose experience anchors the film, what the audience is invited to hope, fear, question or anticipate, the dominant genre promise, intended emotional movement, signature pressure or move and what should remain after the ending.

Plot is what changes. Story is why those changes matter to people. Structure arranges pressure, choice and consequence. Style selects and presents the experience. Theme is the human question tested by that arrangement.

definitions.meaning: The kind of experience, question and payoff the film invites viewers to expect.
A compact reference for promise, genre, tone, question, signatures and ending effect.

example.title: A tense family mystery
example.text: The plot concerns a missing recording. The experience promises intimate suspicion, dry humour and the fear that recovering the truth may end the family.

mistakes: Listing genre without its audience promise.
Treating theme as a slogan.
Confusing plot mechanics with emotional experience.
lessons.exercise: Create the active project's Story Experience Card and find one current field or screenplay image that proves each line.

lessons.title: Control Pacing Through Change
lessons.overview: Measure pacing by the rate and pattern of meaningful change—not genre speed, action quantity or page count alone.
objectives: Track meaningful change.
Use compression, expansion and release.
Compare planned and observed movement.

sections.heading: Change creates pace
paragraphs: Track frequency and size of condition changes, urgency, information reveal or reinterpretation, tactic changes, reversals, sentence and scene density, visual duration, silence, transitions, handoffs and audience processing time.
A quiet scene may move quickly if a relationship changes irreversibly. An action sequence may feel slow when it repeats the same obstacle without changing strategy, cost or information.

definitions.meaning: The rate and pattern at which meaningful conditions, information, pressure and anticipation change.
Deliberate space that lets the audience process, contrast or anticipate.

example.title: Fast quiet scene
example.text: A mother silently signs away guardianship in forty seconds. Nothing physically large happens, but status, belonging and future options change at once.

checklist: Repeated obstacles change strategy or cost.
mistakes: Assuming comedy is fast and drama slow.
Treating constant intensity as good pacing.
Using estimated length as the only signal.
lessons.exercise: Map pressure, information change, emotional intensity, tone and handoff across the active Block's scenes.

lessons.title: Design Tone Without Monotony
lessons.overview: Treat tone as the story's attitude toward people, events and consequences, expressed through evidence rather than one mood adjective.
objectives: Define tonal promise and range.
Use contrast and controlled turns.
Find tone in evidence.

sections.heading: Attitude, not one mood
paragraphs: Tone comes from point of view, narrative distance, consequence, image, sound, rhythm, diction and character-specific carriers. Humour can exist inside darkness and seriousness inside comedy.
Tonal rupture is usually caused by inconsistent consequence or point of view, not emotional variety. Tone may evolve as the story changes.

definitions.meaning: The work's attitude toward its people, events and consequences.
A shift that breaks the established point of view or consequence logic without purposeful preparation.

example.title: Humour under threat
example.text: A frightened medic keeps correcting grammar during an evacuation. The humour reveals control strategy; casualties still carry full consequence.

checklist: The ending evolves or fulfils the promise.
mistakes: Demanding one emotion throughout.
Using adjectives without images or behaviour.
Calling any contrast inconsistent.
lessons.exercise: Identify an image, action, dialogue rhythm, sound idea and consequence that currently produce the intended tone.

lessons.title: Make Theme a Dramatic Argument
lessons.overview: Develop theme as a contested question tested through beliefs, choices and consequences rather than a moral every element repeats.
objectives: Separate topic and theme.
Map competing answers.
Find choice-and-consequence proof.

sections.heading: The argument stays alive
paragraphs: Define the topic, central question or proposition, anti-theme or competing answer, character beliefs and strategies, evidence that makes more than one answer plausible, choices that test them and consequences that refine or overturn them.

Subplots and relationships can run alternate experiments. The climax may prove, refuse, compromise or tragically fail the emerging answer. The ending image and reflection provide the final interpretive frame.

sections.heading: Contribution without repetition
paragraphs: A scene does not need to state or visibly repeat the theme. It contributes when it changes the conditions under which the question will eventually be answered.
Excessive thematic agreement can make the story preachy and predictable. Unsupported or one-sided arguments are questions for review, not automatic errors.

definitions.meaning: A live human question or contested proposition tested by the story's choices and consequences.
A credible competing answer, strategy or worldview.

example.title: Safety versus truth
example.text: One relationship rewards concealment, another rewards exposure, and the climax forces a choice whose consequence complicates both answers.

mistakes: Announcing the moral.
Making every line repeat the theme.
Giving the counter-answer no credible success.
lessons.exercise: Build a Theme Argument Map linking the active question, two answers, characters, Story Threads, choices, consequences and ending reflection.

lessons.title: Write Scenes That Change Conditions
lessons.overview: Connect entry, purpose, driver, objective, opposition, tactic, pivot, value change, outcome, exit and handoff through Scene Pulse evidence.
objectives: Find the indispensable job.
Create a playable pivot and value change.
Hand consequence forward.

sections.heading: Complete scene movement
paragraphs: Define entry condition, indispensable purpose, driver and immediate objective, opposition or incompatible result, tactic and action, pressure and complication, pivot/discovery/refusal/reversal, changed value or relationship state, outcome, consequence, exit condition and handoff.

A scene does not require a formulaic miniature beginning, middle and end. It must create meaningful change or deliver necessary experience that cannot be achieved more effectively elsewhere. Scene type describes delivery—not purpose.
points: Pressure Lock: The incompatible force that prevents the scene driver from simply obtaining the objective.
Cut Line: The latest useful entry and earliest decisive exit for the scene.
Pivot: A discovery, refusal, interruption or reversal that makes the opening tactic insufficient.
Value flip: A practical, relational or emotional condition that changes between entry and exit.
Handoff: The consequence, question, choice or threat that makes the next movement necessary.

definitions.meaning: The indispensable dramatic job only this scene can perform in its current place.
The result that makes the next movement necessary.

example.title: Reaction scene with a turn
example.text: A character enters planning to hide a death, sees a child repeat the victim's gesture and exits choosing public confession. The scene is quiet but changes strategy, theme and the next objective.

mistakes: Treating dialogue or action as purpose.
Ending after information delivery.
Forcing a formula instead of meaningful change.
lessons.exercise: Use the Scene Pulse overlay on the active scene and run one revision experiment for its weakest term.

lessons.title: Turn Inner Meaning Into Screen Evidence
lessons.overview: Translate internal claims into selected visible, audible or performable evidence while avoiding exhaustive description and routine camera direction.
objectives: Convert abstractions to evidence.
Select meaningful visual and sonic detail.
Use narration intentionally.

sections.heading: Make the claim playable
paragraphs: Translate she feels trapped, he has become his father, the town is losing hope or their relationship changes through action and refusal, altered objective or tactic, objects used differently, spatial distance, blocking, visual contrast, sound, silence, dialogue, subtext, repeated behaviour with variation and performance opportunity.
Voice-over or narration may be used when the device creates meaning unavailable through ordinary scene action. Ordinary action lines cannot simply enter a character's mind.

sections.heading: Selection is visual writing
paragraphs: Visual writing directs attention and dramatic meaning. It does not inventory every object or routinely dictate camera coverage. Choose the action, detail, image or sound that changes audience understanding.
Detailed description is not automatically cinematic. Production shots belong where coverage and continuity need separate planning.

definitions.meaning: Visible, audible or performable material from which the audience can infer story meaning.
An intentional voice, text or formal layer that adds meaning unavailable through ordinary scene action.

example.title: The town is losing hope
example.text: The memorial candle stall changes from honour system to locked cabinet; the church bell stops halfway; nobody looks up.

mistakes: Writing internal thought as fact.
Listing décor instead of action.
Using camera directions for routine clarity.
lessons.exercise: Convert one abstract active-project statement into action, blocking, sound, dialogue/subtext and one repeated detail with changed meaning.

lessons.title: Build Motifs, Symbols and Echoes
lessons.overview: Create recurring meaning through literal introduction, changed repetition, behaviour, consequence and payoff rather than fixed symbol dictionaries.
objectives: Distinguish symbolic techniques.
Track meaning shifts.
Connect visual and sonic continuity.

sections.heading: Pattern through context and change
paragraphs: Distinguish image, recurring detail, motif, symbol, metaphor, visual or sonic rhyme, foreshadowing, setup/payoff, dramatic irony, allegorical design and opening/closing echo.

Introduce the element literally, repeat it under changed circumstances, let behaviour or consequence alter its meaning, then pay it off, reverse it or leave it deliberately unresolved. The pattern should support the story rather than ask the audience to solve a private puzzle.

sections.heading: Meaning is not universal
paragraphs: A colour, object, name or archetype gains meaning through culture, context, repetition and change. Colour design should account for production context, accessibility and variation rather than a universal lookup table.
Foreshadowing is not merely hiding a clue; it creates a later relationship between expectation and consequence.

definitions.meaning: A recurring element whose repetitions accumulate or change meaning.
An element that carries meaning beyond its literal function because the story establishes that relationship.

example.title: The emergency tone
example.text: It first signals safety testing, later interrupts a lie, then fails during the real disaster; the final silence becomes the echo.

mistakes: Using fixed symbol meanings.
Repeating without variation.
Making the pattern legible only to the writer.
lessons.exercise: Create a Motif and Echo Ledger entry with introduction, repetitions, meaning shifts, associated people/places/threads and payoff or unresolved ending.

lessons.title: Use Advanced Screenplay Forms Clearly
lessons.overview: Choose montage, mini-slugs, intercutting, voice extensions, dual dialogue, inserts, transitions and internal Fountain tools for dramatic purpose—not decoration.
objectives: Understand dramatic purpose and readable form.
Preview export behaviour.
Separate spec, production and planning layers.

sections.heading: Technique follows purpose
paragraphs: For each form, identify the dramatic purpose, correct readable form, what Fountain/FDX/PDF preserves, common misuse and whether it belongs in a spec screenplay, production draft or internal planning layer.
More technical notation does not make a screenplay more cinematic. Use only the form needed to clarify action, time, location, simultaneous strands, off-screen delivery or editorial meaning.
points: Secondary heading / mini-slug: Move within an established location without repeating a full master heading.
Montage: Compress a process or transformation through selected images.
Series of shots: Present brief connected images without implying a full dramatic montage arc.
Intercutting: Alternate simultaneous or related action while preserving the relationship between locations.
Phone or remote conversation: Clarify whether participants share a location, are intercut or one side remains unheard.
V.O. and O.S.: Distinguish narration/voice beyond the immediate scene from a speaker physically present but off screen.
Dual dialogue / overlap: Show two speeches intended to occur simultaneously when the overlap matters dramatically.
Insert / on-screen text / selected shot: Direct attention to essential readable information or an image with dramatic meaning.
Transition: Name an editorial relationship when the transition itself creates meaning.
Section, synopsis and note: Organize Fountain drafts and internal planning without becoming screenplay content.
Omission / boneyard: Temporarily remove material while preserving it in the draft source.

sections.heading: Advanced forms
paragraphs: Cover master headings, mini-slugs, continuous movement, montage, series of shots, intercutting, remote conversations, V.O., O.S., dual dialogue, overlap, inserts, on-screen text, selected shots, meaningful transitions, Fountain sections/synopses/notes, omissions and boneyards.
Preview generated text before insertion and preserve manual editing. Internal notes and boneyards may contain private material and should not appear in submission exports.

definitions.meaning: A short secondary heading used after a master location is established.
Fountain syntax that keeps text in source while omitting it from rendered screenplay pages.

example.title: Intercut with consequence
example.text: A remote warning and a silent control-room countdown alternate because each line changes the other location's available choice.

mistakes: Adding transitions after every scene.
Using montage for unrelated events.
Leaving notes in submission pages.
Treating formatting as decoration.
lessons.exercise: Choose one advanced form for the active scene, edit the template and review the generated Fountain-style text before copying it manually.

lessons.title: Run the Essential Craft Audit
lessons.overview: Review promise, causality, character, pressure, scenes, theme, pace, tone, evidence, motifs, dialogue, genre, formatting, continuity and priorities in a deliberate order.
objectives: Diagnose with evidence and questions.
Separate symptoms from root causes.
Create bounded revision priorities.

sections.heading: Why → how → evidence → diagnose → revise
paragraphs: Begin with the intended audience experience and dramatic function, inspect project and screenplay evidence, ask what produced the current result, then choose a focused experiment. The audit does not calculate a universal screenplay score or rewrite automatically.
Revision improves purpose, evidence and execution through focused passes; it does not produce an objectively perfect final draft.

sections.heading: Questions, not verdicts
paragraphs: A quiet scene, long description, repeated motif, unusual format or unresolved question may be deliberate. Findings should cite evidence, name uncertainty and route the writer to the field or engine that can test the concern.
Manual writing and no-AI workflows remain complete. Optional AI may help assemble or compare a bounded pass, but output remains non-canonical until explicit approval.

definitions.meaning: An ordered evidence review used to identify questions, root causes and revision priorities.
A bounded change used to test a specific diagnosis while preserving the original.

example.title: Tension note with a root cause
example.text: The audit finds not that Act Two is slow, but that three scenes repeat the same tactic and handoff without new cost or information. The revision priority becomes leverage change, not arbitrary cutting.

mistakes: Scoring every technique.
Rewriting before diagnosis.
Treating a checklist as a formula.
Calling a draft perfect or final.
lessons.exercise: Run the fourteen-step audit and record three evidence-based questions, one root cause and one bounded next pass.
